en: Therīgāthā 12.1: The Chapter of Sixteen (Soḷasakanipāta), The Verses of the Elder Nun Puṇṇā Puṇṇātherīgāthā I am Puṇṇā, a woman of humble birth, A scavenger’s daughter, born from a lowly womb. But now I have attained the state of a nun, And I dwell in the Teacher’s Dispensation. I was formerly a slave-girl, Born from a womb of servitude. Now I am a nun, Freed from all bonds of slavery. My former name was Puṇṇā; My mother’s name was Puṇṇikā. But now I am known as Puṇṇā, The nun who has reached the goal. “O Sītā, I was a water-carrier;
I always drew water,
terrified by the fear of punishment from my mistresses.”
Abiding in fear of faults in speech,
O brahmin, of whom are you afraid that you always descend into the water?
"With your limbs trembling,
you experience intense cold.
"Truly, lady, you know me well," she said.
Puṇṇikā, you ask about one who performs wholesome karma and obstructs the evil that has been done.
Whether one be old or young,
whoever commits an evil deed— even he,
by the sprinkling of water [in the ritual], [is purified].
“Who indeed told this to you—
someone who does not know it to one who does not know it?”
By means of this water-consecration,
one is liberated from evil karma;
indeed, they shall go to heaven.
All frogs and turtles,
nāgas and crocodiles, and whatever other creatures move in the water.
Dog-catchers, pig-butchers,
fishermen, deer-trappers;
thieves and executioners.
And those others who have committed evil deeds—
even they are liberated from their evil karma by the sprinkling of water.
If these rivers could carry away the great evil you have done in the past,
they would also carry away your merit.
Therefore you are an outsider.
O Brahmin, you who, out of fear,
always descend into the water;
“O Brahmā, do not strike me;
do not let the cold destroy your skin.
“I am one who has entered upon a wrong path,” [he said].
You have attained the Noble Path;
you have become one who is consecrated by water— this garment I give to you.
“Let this garment be yours alone;
I do not desire the garment.
If you fear suffering, [then give it to me].”
If suffering is unpleasant to you,
do not commit an evil deed,
whether in public or in private.
If you will do, or are doing, an evil deed,
there is no escape from suffering for you.
Even if you flee after having committed [the offense],
if you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you.
Go for refuge to the Buddha,
to the Dhamma, and to the Tathāgata’s Saṅgha;
undertake the precepts of virtuous conduct.
That will be for your benefit.
“I go for refuge to the Buddha,
to the Dhamma, and to the Tathāgata’s Saṅgha;”
I undertake the precepts;
this will be for my welfare.
Formerly, I was a kinsman of Brahmā.
Today I am a true brahmin;
I am one possessed of the three knowledges, perfected in the Vedas,
a learned scholar, and one who has performed the ritual ablutions.
… The Elder Nun Puṇṇā … The Sixteen-Section Chapter is concluded.
